To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the energy dependence of the logarithmic slope of the fusion cross section is partly due to a nonharmonic Coulomb barrier, and 2) the large low-energy fusion cross sections can be explained with large surface diffusiveness.

the energy dependence in the low-energy part of the fusion cross section is mainly due to the shape of the Couloub barrier and that the low-energy slope of the fusion cross sections is consistent with a large surface diffusiveness of the nuclear interaction.

the energy dependence and the magnitude of the logarithmic slope of the fusion excitation function are consistent with the asymmetric shape of both the Coulomb and the nuclear barriers and the large surface diffusiveness of nuclei.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the nuclear interaction at extreme sub-barrier energies.
the fusion reaction at deep subbarrier energies.
the fusion of two nuclei at very low energies, where the Coulomb barrier is so large that the two nuclei are barely touching each other.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence for any anomalous fusion behavior in the sub-barrier region.
the experimental data at extreme subbarriers are in agreement with theory.
the observed steep excitation functions are not a contradiction of theory but rather the consequence of a combination of experimental and theoretical uncertainties.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the large low energy slopes are not a problem but a solution.
the large slope of the excitation function is a manifestation of the large surface diffusivity, and that the latter is the main cause for the observed large cross sections at extreme low energies.
the observed energy dependence of the fusion cross section slope is not a new effect, but a consequence of the asymmetric shape of fusion barriers and the surface diffuseness of the potential.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the low-energy fusion excitation function is not only a function of the Coulomb potential but also a function of the nuclear potential, which can be used to extract nuclear properties.
the low-energy slope of the fusion excitation function is a sensitive probe of the shape of the barrier.
fusion cross sections at deep sub-barrier energies cannot be used to extract information on the nuclear interaction at short range, as is commonly done.
